target_output:
The short answer is that the stomach doesn't differentiate between "old" and "new" food based on time. Instead, it differentiates based on **size and consistency**. 

The stomach doesn't pass food into the small intestine based on a timer; it acts more like a blender with a very fine strainer at the bottom. 

Here is exactly how the stomach manages this process, even if you eat every 30 minutes:

### 1. The "Strainer" (The Pyloric Sphincter)
At the bottom of the stomach is a muscular valve called the **pyloric sphincter**, which connects the stomach to the small intestine. This valve only opens a tiny bit—just enough to let particles that are **1 to 2 millimeters in size** pass through. 
* **Older food** has been churned with stomach acid and enzymes into a smooth, milky liquid called *chyme*. Because it is a liquid, it easily slips through the pyloric valve.
* **Newer food** is still in solid chunks. When the stomach muscles squeeze to push food out, the liquid chyme passes through, but the solid chunks of new food hit the narrow valve and bounce back into the stomach to be ground up some more. This bouncing back is a process called *retropulsion*.

### 2. The Layering Effect
The stomach is not just one big mixing bowl; it has distinct regions. 
* The upper part of the stomach (the **fundus** and body) acts as a storage area. 
* The lower part of the stomach (the **antrum**) is the heavy-duty grinder. 
When you eat, the new food tends to settle in the upper part of the stomach, layering on top of the food that is already there. The stomach slowly feeds the food from the top "storage" area down into the bottom "grinding" area. So, if you eat a snack 30 minutes after a meal, the new snack mostly waits in the upper stomach while the older meal is being processed at the bottom.

### 3. Hormonal Feedback Loops
If you continuously eat every 30 minutes, your digestive system has a built-in communication network to prevent a traffic jam. 
As the older, liquefied food enters the small intestine, the intestine detects the calories, fats, and acids. If the small intestine is busy processing that food, it releases hormones (like CCK and secretin) that send a signal back to the stomach. 
This signal tells the stomach: *"I am full right now. Stop sending food."* The stomach will then slow down its muscular contractions and delay emptying until the small intestine is ready for the next batch.

### Summary Analogy
Imagine a funnel with a sieve at the bottom. If you pour in a mixture of water and ice cubes, the water (old, digested food) will flow right through the sieve. The ice cubes (new, undigested food) will stay in the funnel until they melt down to a small enough size to pass through. It doesn't matter if you keep adding more ice cubes every 30 minutes; only the melted liquid will ever make it through the exit.

**1. The "Liquid Fast Pass" (The Magenstrasse)**
Let’s say at 12:00 PM you eat a dense, heavy steak. That is going to take 3 to 4 hours to break down. Then, at 1:00 PM, you drink a smoothie or eat some easily dissolving watermelon. 
The new smoothie does not sit at the top of the stomach waiting for the steak to finish. The stomach has a specialized groove along its inner curve called the **gastric canal** (or *magenstrasse*, which is German for "stomach street"). Liquids and easily dissolved foods bypass the solid food, run right down this "fast pass" lane, and exit the stomach into the small intestine almost immediately. The new food beats the old food.

**2. The Macronutrient Race**
Even with solid foods, the stomach plays favorites based on what the food is made of. 
* **Carbohydrates** break down into liquid mush very quickly.
* **Proteins** take longer.
* **Fats** take the longest.

If you eat a piece of fatty pork (old food), and then 45 minutes later you eat a handful of saltine crackers (new food), those crackers will turn to liquid chyme and slip through the valve at the bottom of the stomach while the pork is still bouncing around inside, waiting to be ground down.

Honestly... yes. You are exactly right. 

If you are eating a standard diet, the stomach's mechanics absolutely function as "differentiating by age with extra steps." 

For the vast majority of our meals, the food that goes in first goes to the bottom, gets ground up first, turns to liquid first, and leaves first. From a practical, everyday perspective, the stomach is running a chronological queue. 

The reason biologists and doctors focus on those "extra steps" (consistency and size) instead of just calling it an age-based queue is because of what would happen if the stomach *actually* tracked age.

Think of it like a **coin sorting machine**. 
If you drop a handful of quarters into a coin sorter one by one, the first quarter you drop in will be the first one to roll out the bottom. It looks exactly like the machine is sorting them by age—first in, first out. 
But the machine doesn't know about time; it only knows about the *size* of the hole the quarter falls through. (And if you drop a smaller dime in last, it will fall through its hole and beat the older quarters to the bottom). 

The stomach is just a biological coin sorter. Gravity and anatomy ensure that the oldest food is usually at the bottom getting processed, which makes it look and act like it's sorting by age. 

But the body *needs* those extra steps—the physical sorting—because a strict age-based system would be dangerous. If the stomach operated like a conveyor belt that simply dumped whatever was at the end of the line every 2 hours, it would eventually dump a completely undigested, solid chunk of food into the small intestine, which could cause a life-threatening bowel obstruction. 

So, to your point: yes, for all practical purposes, the stomach treats older food differently because it arrived first and has been at the bottom of the pile the longest. The "extra steps" are just biology's way of enforcing that chronological queue without accidentally killing you in the process!
